title: Updates, patches and end-of-life devices
body_md:
## An update closes a known door, if it installs

The switch in settings says “Automatic updates: on.” The phone has also been waiting for a restart since last month, and the newest security patch on it is older than that.

A security patch closes a flaw that a web page, a document, an app or someone holding your device could otherwise use. Updating will not stop a scammer from talking you into something, and it cannot fix flaws nobody has found yet, but an old, vulnerable version keeps open a door that a fix would already have shut. Turn on automatic updates for the operating system (OS), the browser, your apps and your router’s firmware, wherever they exist. Then check that they finish. A device can be short of storage, power, Wi-Fi or a restart, and an “auto update” toggle does not prove the last patch went in. Look at the system’s update screen or the maker’s official app, and never install an update package that arrives in an unexpected message.

Before a big update, back up your data and make sure you know how to get it back. Install urgent security fixes promptly, as the vendor advises. A feature upgrade that might disturb software you need for work is another matter: check compatibility and pick a short maintenance window. Be wary of any rule of the “patch within exactly seven days” kind, since urgency and rollout timing differ from fix to fix. And if a trusted app says it needs a newer OS than your device can run, look at the maker’s support page rather than downloading a “compatibility patch” from a third party.

## Support belongs to an exact product

End of support means the vendor no longer supplies ordinary security fixes for that product or version. The device still switches on and runs its apps, but that does not make it a good home for your primary email, your banking or your password manager. Some vendors release a limited fix as an exception, or run an extended-update program, so check the exact model, edition and enrollment.

Windows 10 makes a clear case. Ordinary support ended on 14 October 2025. Microsoft’s consumer Extended Security Updates (ESU) is a separate, temporary path for eligible devices that have enrolled, and a PC that merely says Windows 10 is not thereby receiving ESU. For Windows 10 version 22H2, Microsoft says its KB5126256 licensing preparation package is a prerequisite: it is neither enrollment nor a security update, and consumers and organizations follow their own enrollment routes and edition rules. Apple and Android support also depend on the model, so beware of rules like “every iPhone older than five years is unsupported.”

For an unsupported device, move the sensitive tasks first, to a supported replacement or upgrade. If you cannot replace it right away, cut its exposure: take high-value accounts off it, avoid untrusted downloads, switch off network services you don’t use and, for an IoT device, put it on a guest network, provided your router really keeps the clients apart. That kind of segmentation limits some movement across the network. It cannot patch the device, protect its cloud account or promise containment. Cameras and routers with no firmware updates deserve a place on your list, because they can sit online unnoticed. A factory reset does not create new security support. Once your data has moved, plan to retire the device or use it offline, and check your backups before wiping anything.

widget_config.goal: Find out whether a device is actually receiving security fixes, install a pending update safely, and have a practical plan for equipment that no longer gets any.
widget_config.today_action: On one phone or laptop, open the built-in update screen, check the installed version and any pending restart, confirm a recent backup, and schedule the next security update. Write down one old device whose support status you still need to check.
widget_config.scope: General device advice, checked 2026-10-20. Vendor support differs by exact model, OS edition and ESU enrollment. Windows 10 dates are given only for the consumer editions they apply to, and the NCSC documents are written for UK organizations. The cases are invented.

blocks.title: The old camera that still streams
blocks.situation: A home camera still works, but its maker lists the exact model as unsupported and offers no firmware updates. It shares a network with the family’s laptops.
blocks.analysis: A sharp picture says nothing about patches. The family plans a supported replacement, removes remote access it does not need, moves the camera to the guest network and checks that this network really keeps clients apart until the switch. Isolation lowers some of the risk. It does not make the camera itself secure.

blocks.title: A delay with a good reason
blocks.situation: A clinic laptop runs a vendor-certified medical app. Mid-shift the system offers a feature upgrade of the OS, while a security patch and a backup are both still pending.
blocks.analysis: Staff do not accept the upgrade mid-shift, and they do not interrupt care. They confirm the update in system settings, make a backup, apply the security fix promptly in an approved window, and settle the feature upgrade with the app vendor and the administrator. A short, managed delay is not the same as neglect without end.

blocks.title: A household’s patch day
blocks.setup: Three invented devices, three different decisions: a laptop, a phone and an old camera. Nothing is actually installed here.

steps.prompt: The phone says automatic updates are on, but its last security patch is old. What do you check?

choices.text: Check storage, power, Wi-Fi and any pending restart, in the official settings.
choices.consequence: You find out why a setting that was on did not finish the job.
choices.explanation: Verify what is installed, not just the toggle.

choices.text: Nothing; automatic updates keep the phone current.
choices.explanation: Automatic processes can fail, or wait for conditions to be met.

steps.prompt: A message urges you to install a “critical browser patch,” and the installer is attached.

choices.text: Run the attachment, since it says critical.
choices.consequence: The file may be malware that has nothing to do with your browser.
choices.explanation: Urgent wording does not authenticate a package.

choices.text: Update through the browser itself or the official system channel.
choices.explanation: The real update path is built into the product.

steps.prompt: The camera’s exact model is no longer supported. What is the lasting fix?

choices.text: Replace it with a supported model and move its settings across safely.
choices.consequence: Your online device can receive fixes again.
choices.explanation: Isolation lowers risk for a while. It is not a patch.

choices.text: Factory reset it every month, indefinitely.
choices.consequence: The known flaws still have no fix.
choices.explanation: A reset does not extend vendor support.

steps.prompt: A laptop on Windows 10 version 22H2 is said to be covered by ESU. How do you check?

choices.text: Take it on trust that every Windows 10 device is covered.
choices.consequence: The device may be unsupported all the same.
choices.explanation: Being eligible for ESU and being enrolled in it are two different facts.

choices.text: Verify the exact edition, eligibility, enrollment and recently installed updates in Microsoft and Windows settings.
choices.consequence: Coverage is shown by actual enrollment and by what has been installed.
choices.explanation: An ESU option, or a preparation package, is not enrollment.

blocks.debrief: Replay it and keep four things apart: an update that is available, one that is installed, the vendor’s support, and a stopgap for a device with none.

blocks.title: Take it to your own devices

questions.prompt: Automatic updates are on, but the device has not restarted in weeks. What should you check?

choices.text: The pending restart and the installed patch version, in system settings.
choices.explanation: Some patches wait for a restart or another condition.

choices.text: Nothing; the setting proves every patch is installed.
choices.explanation: A setting that is switched on has not necessarily finished its work.

questions.prompt: An unsupported device still works perfectly. What does that tell you?

choices.text: That it is safe for all your sensitive accounts.
choices.explanation: Working software can still carry known flaws.

choices.text: That it may keep running while missing ordinary security fixes.
choices.explanation: Working and being supported are separate things.

questions.prompt: A guest network keeps an old camera apart from your laptops. What is left to worry about?

choices.text: The camera itself, and its cloud account, can still be exposed.
choices.explanation: Separating the network narrows some local routes, but the camera’s own flaws remain.

choices.text: Nothing; every security problem is solved.
choices.explanation: Separating the network is one layer among several.

questions.prompt: A PC on Windows 10 version 22H2 has installed the KB5126256 ESU preparation update. Does that mean it is enrolled?

choices.text: Yes, the preparation package brings coverage with it.
choices.explanation: All it does is prepare the device.

choices.text: No; verify actual enrollment and the security updates received.
choices.explanation: Microsoft treats the prerequisite and ESU enrollment as separate steps.
